keySentence: Pinocchio told lies to avoid consequences.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Every time Pinocchio got in trouble he made up a story. He told the fairy he had gone to school when he had not. He told Geppetto he had studied hard when he had lost his books. Each lie felt like an escape door he could slip through. But every door led to a smaller and harder room than before. One lie about the theater sent him into the belly of a shark. Pinocchio told lies to avoid consequences.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Every time Pinocchio got into trouble his first instinct was to invent an explanation. He told the fairy he had gone to school when he had spent the day at the puppet theater. He told Geppetto he had studied hard when he had actually lost his school books gambling. Each lie felt like an escape — a door he could slip through to avoid being punished. But the door always led to a room that was smaller and more difficult than the one before. The lie about the theater led to being swallowed by a shark in the middle of the wide sea. Pinocchio kept choosing the quick and easy path and kept arriving at harder and harder places. Pinocchio told lies to avoid consequences.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Every single time Pinocchio found himself in some kind of trouble, his immediate and automatic instinct was to invent a convenient explanation for whatever had happened. He told the blue-haired fairy that he had been to school, when in fact he had spent the entire afternoon watching the traveling puppet theater and enjoying himself thoroughly. He told Geppetto that he had studied hard with his new books, when in reality he had lost the books gambling with some much more experienced boys outside the marketplace. Each individual lie, in the moment of telling it, felt like an escape hatch — a conveniently located door he could slip through to avoid being punished or questioned. But the door always led, somehow, to another room smaller and more difficult than the one he had just been trying to escape from. The particular lie about the puppet theater, for example, led him on a strange journey that ended with him being swallowed by an enormous shark in the middle of the open sea. Pinocchio kept choosing the quick and easy path whenever it was offered to him, and as a direct result he kept arriving at harder and harder and more desperate places. Every lie was a short-term rescue that became, over time, a long-term catastrophe. Pinocchio told lies to avoid consequences.
